subject: Business
title: Post-Agreement: Protecting the Deal
description: A 60-second lesson on Post-Agreement: Protecting the Deal.

hook.text: You shook hands on a deal. Three weeks later, they say they 'remember it differently.' No contract exists.

buildup.text: A verbal agreement isn't a deal until it's documented, signed, and enforceable.

discovery.text: Summarize terms in writing immediately after the handshake, while both sides' memories are fresh.

twist.text: Ambiguous language in contracts creates future disputes. 'Reasonable effort' means different things to each side.

climax.text: Include specific timelines, metrics, and consequences for non-performance. Remove all wiggle room.

punchline.text: If it's not in writing, it's not a deal.

quiz.question: Why should terms be documented immediately after a handshake?
options: Memories diverge quickly and ambiguity creates disputes
Verbal agreements are always legally binding
It speeds up the next negotiation

details.summary: Post-agreement negotiation explores whether both parties can improve a deal after reaching initial agreement, and deal protection ensures commitments are honored through clear documentation, accountability mechanisms, and relationship management. Many deals fail in implementation, not negotiation.

takeaways: Post-agreement negotiation can improve deals both parties have already accepted
Clear documentation and accountability mechanisms protect implementation
Many well-negotiated deals fail because implementation is not carefully managed

faq.question: What is post-agreement negotiation and how does it add value?
faq.answer: After reaching an initial agreement, both parties explore whether adjustments could make the deal even better for both sides. With the pressure of no-deal removed, people are more creative. Improvements found at this stage feel like bonuses, strengthening the relationship and the agreement.

faq.question: How do you protect a deal during implementation?
faq.answer: Document all terms clearly and specifically. Define milestones and review points. Create escalation procedures for disputes. Maintain the relationship through regular check-ins. Address small issues before they become large ones. Build in flexibility for unforeseen circumstances.
